title: Rollinsville Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: See Rollinsville well depths, yields, water levels, and drilling costs, including a 220-foot median and finished-well estimates.
h1: Rollinsville Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land around Rollinsville means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and water supplies that can change from one lot to the next. Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of Rollinsville provide a useful local starting point, but they do not replace a site-specific well investigation.

Most permitted wells here serve domestic or household use. The records point to fractured-bedrock conditions rather than a broad, predictable basin aquifer. Check nearby permits, construction details, water levels, and yields before you commit to a property or finalize a building plan.

sections.heading: Rollinsville well depth: plan for fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median well depth around Rollinsville is 220 feet. The middle half runs from 120 to 352 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median may not cover the conditions on your lot. One well in the records reaches 1,202 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet.

Depths vary because the local permits primarily identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records include 3,138 wells in that category, along with 30 in Fractured Crystalline and 15 in Fractured Granite. For budgeting, ask the driller to show the per-foot rate, the assumed drilling depth, and what happens if the hole must continue.

Nearby records from Nederland, Bonanza Mountain Estates, Eldora, and St. Ann Highlands can help establish local context, but the closest comparable wells are the most useful.

sections.heading: What Rollinsville wells produce
sections.html:
Among wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. A large share, 64%, falls between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 25% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Only 2% report less than 1 gallon per minute, but that small percentage matters when you are comparing individual properties. A lower-yield well may still work with adequate storage and a properly designed pump system, but it can affect household use and recovery between uses. The records show 8% above 15 gallons per minute.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, accounting for 94% of the records. Confirm the permitted use and pumping limits before assuming the well can support irrigation or other demands.

sections.heading: Water levels around Rollinsville and what the record shows
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 40 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 20 and 61 feet. That is the water level while the well is at rest, not the pumping level. A contractor still needs to evaluate drawdown, recovery, pump setting, and storage.

The decade series does not show a simple, steadily dropping water table. Median reported depth to water was 32 feet in the 1960s, 25 feet in the 1970s, 50 feet in the 2010s, and 40 feet in the 2020s. Measurements are available from only 188 wells, and the wells measured in each period may not represent the same locations.

Use the nearby measurements as clues, not a guarantee. A well close to your lot, in similar ground and at a similar elevation, is more informative than a regional average.

sections.heading: Who drilled near Rollinsville, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity spans several generations. The records show 38 permits from the 1950s, 197 from the 1960s, 584 from the 1970s, 393 from the 1980s, 666 from the 1990s, 448 from the 2000s, 237 from the 2010s, and 148 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently represented drillers are Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) with 573 records, C. R. Smith Drilling (Smith, Calvin R.) with 478, and C R Smith Drilling Inc (Smith, Frank) with 450. A permit listing shows historical activity, not a recommendation or a guarantee that a company is currently available.

When reviewing a property, pull the original permit and construction record. Compare the listed depth, casing, grout, pump yield, and static water level with the seller’s description.

sections.heading: Rollinsville well drilling cost at the median depth
sections.html:
Rollinsville drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate used for this area is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 220-foot median depth, the drilled hole estimates to about $14,300 to $22,000.

A finished system with the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $20,300 to $34,000 at that median depth. This is a planning range, not a fixed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grouting requirements, pump changes, or additional trenching can move the final price.

Request an itemized proposal before building your budget. It should separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, storage, trenching, electrical work, testing, and permit-related services so you can compare bids accurately.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Fractured rock can produce a good well on one parcel and a poor result nearby. Review the 3,253 wells in the local permit scope, paying particular attention to the 1,045 that report pump yield and the 188 that report static water level. A dry hole or low-yield result is not ruled out by a strong median.

Water quality also deserves its own investigation. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,446 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove contamination at your property. Test the actual well, and discuss appropriate testing with a qualified water professional.

Check septic setbacks, replacement-area options, slope, access for a drill rig, and the proposed building location. A well and septic system need to work together with the house site.

sections.heading: A practical Rollinsville lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit record for the property and nearby parcels. Compare depths, yields, static levels, construction details, and permitted uses. Look first at wells near the lot, then expand toward Coal Creek and Black Hawk only when you need more context.

For an existing home, obtain a recent flow or yield evaluation, static and pumping water levels, and a laboratory water test. For vacant land, have a driller review access, geology, likely depth, and the location of the house and septic system before you make a final site plan.

Remember that an exempt household-use well has a 35-gpm pumping limit, and over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan. Confirm the actual water right and allowed uses with Colorado DWR. Good records reduce surprises, but they cannot guarantee the result on a new hole.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rollinsville?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Rollinsville is 220 feet. The middle half runs from 120 to 352 feet, while the 90th percentile is 460 feet. Four percent are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,202 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make individual sites variable.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Rollinsville?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 220-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,300 to $22,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,300 to $34,000. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water does a Rollinsville well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-four percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. Have the specific well tested rather than relying on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rollinsville?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. About 10 miles of the area includes 17 PFAS sites, 2,446 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These are screening concerns, not proof of contamination. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory before use.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Rollinsville?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a steady decline. Depth to water was 32 feet in the 1960s, 25 feet in the 1970s, 50 feet in the 2010s, and 40 feet in the 2020s. Only 188 wells report static water levels, and the measured wells may differ by location, so treat the series as limited context.
